Teaching through formulas and conceptual decisions

Count independent local relation choices

For n labeled objects, a relation is an n×n Boolean matrix. There are 2n2 arbitrary relations. Reflexivity fixes all diagonal entries to 1 and leaves n(n-1) free bits. Symmetry ties each off-diagonal pair and leaves n(n+1)/2 independent bits. Combining reflexivity with symmetry leaves only n(n-1)/2 free bits. Antisymmetry forbids only the both-directions state for distinct objects, so every unordered off-diagonal pair has three choices; each diagonal remains independently optional. The antisymmetric count is therefore 2n3n(n-1)/2. Asymmetry additionally forbids every diagonal and has count 3n(n-1)/2.

Transitivity couples several pairs, so these local-choice products do not count transitive relations. Equivalence relations instead correspond to partitions; their count is the Bell number, with a fixed number of classes counted by a Stirling number of the second kind. A class of size k contributes k2 ordered pairs to the relation. Summing class sizes does not count relation edges.

Use Boolean multiplication for composition

With the convention (x,z)∈S∘R when there exists y with xRy and ySz, the matrix entries use OR of AND-products. Multiple witnesses do not create multiplicity in a relation. The transitive closure includes paths of positive length; the reflexive-transitive closure additionally includes zero-length paths, hence the full diagonal. A cycle can make diagonal pairs appear even in the positive-length closure.

Read a Hasse diagram without confusing four extrema

Minimal means no strictly smaller element; least means below every element. Multiple minimal elements can exist but a least element is unique. For a pair, an upper bound must dominate both; a least upper bound must also lie below every common upper bound. If two incomparable minimal upper bounds exist, there is no join. Hasse edges show covers, omitting loops and transitive edges; reachability reconstructs the order. In the divisor order of a positive integer, meet is gcd and join is lcm, both still divisors of the ambient integer.

Mathematical constructions for difficult relation questions

The complete underlying lesson and forty-six tutorials remain. These additional constructions connect the rewritten bank to deeper formula and proof methods. They keep counts of relations, sizes of one relation, classes, paths and total listings separate.

1. Three counting problems with three different objects

For a fixed labelled carrier A of size n, a relation is one subset of its n-squared possible ordered pairs. A question asking how many relations exist counts possible subsets, typically producing an exponential number. A question asking how many pairs belong to one specified relation counts entries that are one, typically producing a polynomial number. A question asking how many equivalence classes exist counts distinct blocks of that particular partition.

An n-by-n equivalence-block arrangement on n-squared elements has n classes, n-squared carrier elements and n-cubed relation pairs. Each block contributes its own Cartesian square. The universal relation on the same carrier would have n-to-the-fourth pairs, because it additionally includes cross-block pairs. One must not square the quotient size when the task asks for the relation's size.

For arbitrary nonempty block sizes b1,…,bk with total N,

|E|=∑i=1kbi2=N+2∑i=1k(bi2).

The second form separates loops from the two orientations of each within-block distinct pair. It proves, in particular, that |E|−N is even. A proposed size with the wrong parity is impossible without inspecting every partition. For N=6, size profiles (3,2,1) and (2,2,1,1) give fourteen and ten pairs respectively, while their quotient sizes are three and four.

2. Local independence stops when an axiom couples entries

For symmetry, one choice determines both directions of a distinct pair; for antisymmetry, its legal states are 00,10,01. These constraints can be handled independently across unordered pairs. Reflexivity or irreflexivity independently fixes the diagonal. This yields binary or ternary product counts because no local decision constrains a different unordered pair.

Transitivity is different. On vertices one, two and three, accepting edges one-to-two and two-to-three can force one-to-three. Thus decisions are coupled. Applying a local-choice power after adding transitivity does not count transitive relations. The appropriate technique can instead enumerate partitions for equivalence, enumerate partial orders with a structural method, or check a fixed matrix's witness triples.

Seriality also couples symmetry-constrained bits. A row must contain a loop or some incident edge, and an off-diagonal symmetric edge satisfies row requirements at both endpoints. On a labelled n-element carrier, the number of symmetric serial relations with optional loops is

∑j=0n(−1)j(nj)2(n−j)(n−j+1)/2.

To derive it, begin with all symmetric matrices and apply inclusion–exclusion to empty-row events. Fixing j vertices to empty removes their loops and every incident edge, leaving an arbitrary symmetric relation on n-j remaining vertices. The remaining exponent counts its diagonals and unordered pairs. This derivation explains why independently choosing nonempty rows would overcount.

3. Difference-defined equivalence is a subgroup theorem

On the entire real line, a condition x∼y⇔x−y∈H is an equivalence exactly when H contains zero and is closed under negation and addition. Reflexivity forces zero; symmetry tests a difference and its negative; transitivity tests the sum of consecutive differences. Conversely these closure properties give each axiom directly. The full carrier is used in the necessity witnesses, so restricting it can change which differences are ever tested.

This method reduces an infinite family question to concrete algebra. For dyadic rationals, placing two terms over a common power-of-two denominator proves closure. For a union of multiples of two and three, the permitted differences two and three sum to the forbidden difference five. One algebraic counterexample becomes a complete three-point relation counterexample.

For allowed residues H inside ℤ/mℤ, the same argument asks whether H is an additive subgroup. If it is, the number of integer classes is its index, m/|H|. After a finite induced restriction, intersect those integer classes with the carrier and discard empty intersections. The pair count then uses the resulting finite block sizes; neither subgroup size nor the original modulus automatically equals the quotient size.

4. Existence algebra and multiplicity algebra are distinct

With source rows, a composition S∘R has entry

MS∘R[i,j]=⋁k=1r(MR[i,k]∧MS[k,j]).

Each middle index k contributes one possible two-edge witness. Boolean OR collapses multiple witnesses to one truth value. Ordinary multiplication instead sums witness indicators and therefore counts witnesses; it gives the same membership after replacing every positive entry by one, but its numerical entries are not Boolean relation entries.

The matrix order is first the source-to-middle matrix, then the middle-to-target matrix. Its dimensions are m-by-r multiplied by r-by-n. Converse transposes the matrices and reverses the relation composition order. Expanding the common witness gives the proof; merely reversing written symbols without checking types is unreliable.

Separate witnesses also explain failed distributivity over intersection. Each of two compositions may reach the same endpoint through a different middle element, while composition of an intersection requires the relevant edge to exist in both operands. Similarly, a path in each positive closure need not be a path using intersection edges. The distinction recurs across both relational algebra and graph reachability.

5. Closures need a path convention and a leastness certificate

Positive closure includes positive-length paths; reflexive transitive closure additionally includes every zero-length self-path. An acyclic directed path has no positive self-return, so its positive closure has no loops. A directed cycle does have positive self-returns. Therefore the diagonal alone cannot tell which convention produced a matrix: it must be interpreted with the input graph and stated operation.

Every positive endpoint path forces its endpoint pair in any transitive superset, by induction on length. This proves leastness of positive closure. Adding all identity pairs proves leastness for reflexive transitive closure. For equivalence closure, add reverse edges first and then use zero-length reachability so that isolated vertices retain their singleton-class loops.

Intersection closure of an axiom does not by itself ensure an extension exists. An input containing a distinct two-way pair has no antisymmetric superset, because adding pairs cannot remove that violation. For a finite partial-order extension, nontrivial directed cycles are the obstruction; harmless original loops are allowed. When no such cycle exists, reflexive transitive reachability is the least partial-order superset.

6. The exponent grid explains divisibility formulas

For a positive integer M=∏r=1kprar, unique prime factorization identifies each divisor with a vector whose r-th coordinate is between zero and ar. Divisibility is coordinatewise comparison. Hence the number of divisor vertices is

V=∏r=1k(ar+1).

A cover increases one coordinate by one and leaves the rest unchanged. In direction r, that coordinate has ar possible starting values and the other coordinates have all their allowed values. Thus

Ecover=∑r=1kar∏s≠r(as+1).

The directions are disjoint, so adding their counts does not overcount an edge. Hasse diagrams omit identity loops and all strict comparisons obtainable through longer upward paths.

Rank equal to the coordinate sum strictly increases along any strict comparison. The maximum possible rank is ∑rar. Incrementing one coordinate at a time from the all-zero vector to the all-maximal vector attains every intermediate rank, so height measured in vertices is 1+∑rar. The number of saturated least-to-greatest chains is the number of increment orderings,

(∑rar)!∏rar!.

Finally, a nonstrict comparable pair chooses its two endpoints independently in each coordinate chain. A length- ar+1 chain has (ar+22) nonstrict ordered comparisons, giving total relation size ∏r(ar+22). Vertex count, cover count, height, longest-chain count and relation size are five different quantities derived from the same grid.

7. Extremal proofs and dynamic programs certify different outcomes

To prove a longest chain, give an upper bound on every chain and a chain attaining it. To prove a minimum chain partition, give a valid partition and an antichain requiring at least that many parts. To prove a supremum, first prove the candidate bounds every subset member, then prove it lies below every ambient upper bound. A computation of a plausible candidate does not discharge these universal obligations.

Counting linear extensions asks for all legal total listings. At each step, a prefix must be an order ideal. A recurrence may count how many legal sequences reach each ideal; it must prove that possible final elements are disjoint and exhaustive and that removing one produces a valid predecessor state. This is different from choosing one longest Hasse path, which can omit most carrier vertices.

The twelve-divisor example has twelve vertices, seventeen covers, sixty nonstrict comparisons, height six, ten saturated longest chains and 462 linear extensions. The last number follows from the finite ideal-state recurrence in Challenge 6. These values provide a concrete check on which mathematical object an examination asks to count, while the full lesson supplies the proofs underlying each object.

Ten solved synthesis challenges for relations and orders

These original problems combine the selected university methods. They supplement all forty-six retained tutorials and the forty-five rewritten bank answers. The mathematical objects, carriers and target counts are specified before each derivation.

Challenge 1. A difference subgroup with a finite carrier restriction

This model uses this solved challenge’s own carrier, parameters and construction.

Task. On the integers, define x∼y when the residue of x−y modulo ten belongs to {0,5}. Prove equivalence, identify the infinite classes, and count the related ordered pairs after restricting the carrier to {0,…,29}.

Solution. A difference has allowed residue if and only if it is divisible by five. Differences zero, negatives and sums therefore remain allowed, proving the three equivalence axioms. The integer classes are the five residue classes modulo five. This is not a ten-class relation merely because its initial description uses modulo ten: the allowed two-element subgroup coarsens those residues.

The finite restriction contains six numbers in each class. Explicitly, class r contains r,r+5,r+10,r+15,r+20,r+25, for 0≤r<5. A block contributes six choices for each endpoint, including its six loops. Consequently there are 5·62=180 ordered related pairs. This is different from the thirty carrier elements and from the universal carrier square of nine hundred pairs. All five finite classes are nonempty, so the quotient still has five elements.

The restriction is induced: both endpoints must belong to the finite interval. Equivalence survives induced restriction, but an infinite pair-count formula would not be a finite numerical answer. Derive the restricted block sizes before counting them.

Challenge 2. Equal partition counts do not determine relation sizes

This model uses this solved challenge’s own carrier, parameters and construction.

Task. Count partitions of a labelled seven-element carrier into blocks of sizes three and four. Then count partitions of a labelled eight-element carrier into two size-four blocks. Compare both partition counts and their relation pair counts.

Solution. In the seven-element problem, choosing the three-element block uniquely determines its complement, so (73)=35. Do not divide by two: the unequal sizes distinguish which selected subset plays that role. Each such equivalence has 32+42=25 pairs.

For eight elements, choosing one four-element block gives (84)=70, but either of the two equal-sized blocks can be selected first. Every partition is counted twice, so 70/2=35. Each resulting equivalence has 42+42=32 pairs. Thus the number of possible relations is thirty-five in both cases, while the size of one relation differs.

The factorial formulas confirm the distinction: 7!/(3!4!)=35 and 8!/((4!)22!)=35. The block-order symmetry factor applies exactly when the equal-size blocks are interchangeable. It does not remove the labels of the carrier elements.

Challenge 3. Symmetric serial relations require inclusion–exclusion

This model uses this solved challenge’s own carrier, parameters and construction.

Task. On a labelled three-element carrier, count relations that are symmetric and serial, with loops allowed. How many remain if transitivity is additionally required?

Solution. A symmetric matrix has three diagonal bits and three unordered-pair bits, hence sixty-four possibilities. Seriality says no row is empty. Let Ei be the event that vertex i has no outgoing edge. Symmetry also removes every incoming edge to that vertex. Fixing one empty row leaves a symmetric relation on two vertices, giving 23=8 possibilities. Fixing two empty rows leaves one optional loop, giving two possibilities. Fixing all three leaves only the empty relation. Inclusion–exclusion therefore gives

64−3·8+3·2−1=45.

This is not the arbitrary directed serial count 73=343: symmetry ties off-diagonal entries and prevents independent row choices.

If a symmetric transitive relation is serial, choose an outgoing witness aRb for each a. Symmetry supplies bRa, and transitivity forces aRa. Thus it becomes reflexive and is an equivalence. Conversely, an equivalence is symmetric, transitive and serial. There are five partitions of three labelled elements: one three-element block, three choices for a two-element block plus singleton, and the all-singleton partition. Hence exactly five of the forty-five relations meet the added condition.

Challenge 4. Transitive closure can destroy intersection equality

This model uses this solved challenge’s own carrier, parameters and construction.

Task. On {a,b,c,d}, take R={(a,b),(b,c)} and S={(a,d),(d,c)}. Compare (R∩S)+ with R+∩S+ and prove the inclusion direction valid for every input pair.

Solution. The original edge sets are disjoint, so their intersection and its positive closure are empty. Closing R adds (a,c) via b; closing S adds the same endpoint pair via d. Their closures have exactly that pair in common. Thus R+∩S+={(a,c)} and equality fails.

For any relations, a path whose every edge belongs to their intersection is simultaneously a path in each operand. Its endpoint pair therefore lies in both closures, proving (R∩S)+⊆R+∩S+. The converse can fail because the two witnesses need not share any intermediate edges. The output closure need not preserve intersections even though the property “is transitive” is preserved under intersections. Those are different assertions about different objects.

Challenge 5. Symmetric and transitive closure order changes the pair count

This model uses this solved challenge’s own carrier, parameters and construction.

Task. On four vertices, let R={(a,b),(a,c),(c,d)}. Let s add reversed edges and t take positive transitive closure. Compute sizes of s(t(R)), t(s(R)), and the least equivalence containing R.

Solution. Positive closure of R contains its three edges and shortcut (a,d); there is no other outgoing continuation and no cycle. Symmetrizing those four edges adds four distinct reverses, giving eight pairs. No loop is included at this step.

Symmetrizing first makes the undirected connection tree a–b, a–c, c–d traversable in both directions. Any vertex can reach any other, and every vertex has a neighboring edge along which it can travel out and back. Positive closure therefore contains all sixteen pairs, including four loops. The least equivalence is also the universal relation, because these original connections force one class containing all four vertices.

The noncommuting results are eight versus sixteen. A transitivity witness missing from the smaller relation is bRaRc without bRc. Adding only reflexive loops to that eight-pair relation would still leave this missing shortcut. The order of operations has mathematical consequences beyond the diagonal convention.

Challenge 6. Linear extensions of the twelve-divisor grid

This model uses this solved challenge’s own carrier, parameters and construction.

Task. For divisors of 72=2332 under divisibility, find height, width and the number of linear extensions. Derive a finite recurrence for the last count rather than interpreting a single Hasse path as a total listing.

Solution. Exponent coordinates form a four-by-three grid. Rank i+j increases along each strict comparison, so height is six, attained by 1,2,4,8,24,72. Keeping j fixed partitions the grid into three chains, so width is at most three. The three vertices with coordinates (2,0),(1,1),(0,2) are mutually incomparable, attaining width three.

A prefix of a linear extension must be an order ideal: if a divisor has been listed, every strictly smaller divisor has already been listed. Describe the occupied lengths of the j=0,1,2 rows by (a,b,c), where 0≤c≤b≤a≤4. Each row is a prefix because comparison along that row is a chain; the inequalities express the downward comparisons between rows.

Let F(a,b,c) count legal prefix listings of exactly that ideal. The empty listing has F(0,0,0)=1. Remove the last listed vertex. It must be maximal in the ideal and can be the last vertex of row zero when a>b, of row one when b>c, or of row two when c>0. Thus

F(a,b,c)=1a>bF(a−1,b,c)+1b>cF(a,b−1,c)+1c>0F(a,b,c−1),

with omitted terms treated as zero. The final-vertex choices are disjoint and exhaustive, proving the recurrence rather than guessing it from a pattern.

Evaluating states by increasing a+b+c gives F(1,1,1)=1, F(2,2,2)=5, F(3,3,3)=42 and F(4,4,4)=462. Therefore there are 462 linear extensions. By contrast, a saturated path from the least to greatest divisor contains only six of the twelve vertices and has ten possible increment orderings. The counts 462 and ten concern different objects: a total legal listing of all tasks versus one longest chain.

Challenge 7. Intersect partitions, then close their union

This model uses this solved challenge’s own carrier, parameters and construction.

Task. On {1,…,6}, equivalence E has blocks {1,2,3},{4,5,6} and equivalence F has blocks {1,4},{2,5},{3,6}. Find the pair counts of E, F, their intersection, their union and the union's equivalence closure.

Solution. E has 2·32=18 pairs, while F has 3·22=12. An E-block intersects each F-block in exactly one element. The common refinement is therefore six singleton blocks; |E∩F|=6. Inclusion–exclusion gives |E∪F|=18+12−6=24.

Each F-block provides a bridge between the two E-blocks. Since an equivalence already relates all elements inside an E-block, one bridge forces both blocks to merge in any equivalence extension. The closure thus has a single six-element block and thirty-six pairs, adding twelve pairs to the unclosed union.

A direct missing-pair witness is 1 related to 2 by E and 2 related to 5 by F, while 1 and 5 are in neither a common E-block nor a common F-block. Transitivity fails before closing. Sum-of-squares counts apply to the equivalence operands and their equivalence closure; they cannot be applied to the union as if its overlapping original blocks were a partition.

Challenge 8. Boolean composition and numerical witness counts

This model uses this solved challenge’s own carrier, parameters and construction.

Task. Source A and middle B each have three elements, and target C has two. In the specified orders, matrices are

MR=(110011101),MS=(101101).

Compute S∘R and distinguish its number of pairs from the number of two-edge witnesses.

Solution. Numerical multiplication gives

MRMS=(211211).

The first row's first entry is two because middle vertices one and two both reach the first target. The second row's second entry is two because its middle vertices two and three both reach the second target. Each other entry has exactly one witness.

Boolean multiplication replaces addition by OR and multiplication by AND. Every numerical entry is positive, so the Boolean result is the three-by-two all-one matrix. Hence all six endpoint pairs belong to S∘R, while summing numerical entries counts eight two-edge witnesses. Repeated witnesses do not duplicate membership in a set of pairs.

The symbol order of S∘R does not reverse the source-row matrix order: it is MR followed by MS. A two-by-three matrix cannot be substituted for the given second matrix without changing the typed carriers. Establish dimensions and the witness definition before doing arithmetic.

Challenge 9. Lexicographic descent without a fixed positive linear rank

This model uses this solved challenge’s own carrier, parameters and construction.

Task. A procedure on natural pairs may call (m,n−2) when n≥2, or (m−1,n2+1) when m>0. Each call returns before a fixed finite amount of subsequent work finishes, and each invocation makes at most these two calls. Prove termination. Can a rank am+bn with fixed positive a,b certify every allowed call?

Solution. The first call preserves m and reduces n. The second strictly reduces m, so its possibly much larger second coordinate does not prevent lexicographic descent. Natural-number order is well-founded; choosing a least occurring first coordinate and then least occurring second coordinate proves the lexicographic order well-founded.

Use well-founded induction on argument pairs. Assuming all smaller invocations terminate, both guarded recursive calls terminate; only finitely many calls and subsequent steps occur, so this invocation terminates. Guards preserve nonnegative coordinates. This proves completion of the recursion tree, not merely termination of one arbitrarily chosen branch.

For the second call, the linear rank change is −a+b(n2+1−n). With fixed positive a,b, choose n sufficiently large to make this positive. Taking m=1 still permits that call. Thus no such fixed positive linear rank certifies all transitions. The absence of this particular rank does not refute termination; the lexicographic relation supplies the actual proof.

Challenge 10. Changing the carrier changes a join and distributivity

This model uses this solved challenge’s own carrier, parameters and construction.

Task. Delete divisor six from the divisor lattice of twelve, leaving {1,2,3,4,12} under divisibility. Is the resulting poset a lattice? Find the join of two and three, and test one distributive identity.

Solution. The remaining shape is a chain 1<2<4<12, plus vertex three strictly between bottom one and top twelve and incomparable with two and four. Every comparable pair has its smaller member as meet and larger member as join. The only incomparable pairs are (2,3) and (4,3); both have meet one and join twelve. This exhaustive pair classification proves it is a lattice.

The join of two and three is twelve, not their numerical lcm six, because six is absent from the carrier. Twelve is the only common upper bound still available, so it satisfies both the upper-bound and leastness obligations. A formula from a larger ambient lattice must not silently insert a missing object.

Now take a=4,b=2,c=3. Then b∨c=12, giving a∧(b∨c)=4. But a∧b=2 and a∧c=1, so (a∧b)∨(a∧c)=2∨1=2. The unequal outputs four and two disprove distributivity. This five-element pentagon lattice is finite and therefore complete under the chapter's nonempty-lattice convention; completeness does not imply distributivity.

Detailed derivation tutorials

The following complete proofs and implementations support the new examination problems. They develop the reasoning needed to derive formulas; the separately labeled examination bank below tests calculation, concepts and distractor decisions.

The following problems are grouped by method, not by increasing intimidation. Read each solution as a short lesson: identify the object and hypotheses, carry out the argument, then inspect the stated trap. Original means authored for this chapter. Course-derived identifies the source of the mathematical exercise pattern; instances and explanations are independently written. None is a request to test the student before reading.

Tutorial 1. A carrier changes a verdict

Original; method: inspect the declared type. Let R = {(1,u),(2,u)}. Compare the relation from {1,2} to {u,v} with the relation from {1,2,3} to {u,v}. Is either a total function or a surjection?

Solution. Each listed first coordinate has exactly one output, so both relations are right-unique. The first carrier has no unused input, making its relation a total function. The second leaves 3 without an output, making its relation only a partial function. Both have range {u}, so neither is surjective onto {u,v}. Reducing the target carrier to {u} would change the surjectivity verdict. The pair set alone does not settle properties that quantify over carriers.

Tutorial 2. Counting typed relations and functions

Course-derived: Cambridge, exercise 3; extended counting. For a three-element source and a two-element target, count all relations, left-total relations, partial functions, and total functions. Also count ternary relations on carriers of sizes 2, 3, and 4.

Solution. There are six binary pair positions, giving 26 = 64 relations. Each of three rows may choose any of three nonempty target subsets, giving 33 = 27 left-total relations. A partial-function row has three choices, namely no output or either target, so there are also 27 partial functions. These equal numerical counts represent different families. A total-function row has two choices, giving 23 = 8. A ternary relation is a subset of a Cartesian product with 2·3·4 = 24 triples, giving 224 possibilities. Being ternary does not force one output per input pair.

Tutorial 3. Why relational images lose intersections

Original; method: distinguish witnesses. Let R = {(a,z),(b,z)}, X = {a}, and Y = {b}. Compute the images needed to test intersection preservation. Test inverse-image preservation too.

Solution. Both R[X] and R[Y] equal {z}, but X ∩ Y is empty and its image is empty. Thus the relational-image inclusion can be strict. For inverse images, choose T = {(p,u),(p,v)} and disjoint target sets {u},{v}. Each inverse image is {p}, whereas the inverse image of the empty intersection is empty. A function's inverse image avoids this failure because one input cannot witness two different target values. Relations have no such uniqueness condition.

Tutorial 4. Compose through a common middle carrier

Course-derived: Cambridge, exercise 1. Let A = {1,2,3}, B = {u,v,w}, C = {x,y}, R = {(1,u),(1,v),(2,w),(3,v)}, and S = {(u,x),(v,x),(v,y)}. Compute S ∘ R and its Boolean matrix.

Solution. From input 1, the middle objects u,v reach x, and v also reaches y. Input 2 reaches only w, which has no outgoing S edge, so it contributes no pair. Input 3 reaches v and therefore reaches both targets. The result is { (1,x),(1,y),(3,x),(3,y) }. In the stated row and column orders, the output matrix rows are (1,1), (0,0), (1,1). Two middle witnesses for (1,x) still produce one relation pair; Boolean disjunction does not count them twice.

Tutorial 5. Composition is not commutative

Original; method: find an endpoint pair. On {a,b,c} let R = {(a,b)} and S = {(b,c)}. Compare the two compositions.

Solution. Following R then S gives the single chain a → b → c, so S ∘ R = {(a,c)}. Following S first reaches c, where no R edge starts, so R ∘ S is empty. Both compositions are well-typed, yet unequal. Associativity concerns grouping three steps; it says nothing about exchanging two steps.

Tutorial 6. Composition does not distribute over intersection

Original; method: compare shared and separate witnesses. From {a} to {b,c} take R = {(a,b)} and T = {(a,c)}. From {b,c} to {z} take S = {(b,z),(c,z)}. Compare S ∘ (R ∩ T) with (S ∘ R) ∩ (S ∘ T).

Solution. The input intersection is empty because the two edges differ, so its composition is empty. Each separate composition contains (a,z), one through b and the other through c. Their intersection therefore contains that pair. The right side permits different middle witnesses; the left side requires a middle edge in both input relations. The analogous inclusion always holds, but equality requires additional conditions.

Tutorial 7. Converse identities by pair membership

Course-derived: Cambridge, exercise 5. Prove that converse preserves intersection and union and reverses composition.

Solution. A pair (b,a) is in (R ∩ S) − 1 exactly when (a,b) belongs to both R and S. This is exactly membership in R − 1 ∩ S − 1. Replace “both” by “at least one” to obtain the union identity. For composition, (c,a) belongs to (S ∘ R) − 1 precisely when some b satisfies aRbSc. Reversing the two edges gives cS − 1bR − 1a, which is membership in R − 1 ∘ S − 1. The order reversal is compelled by the witness chain, not by a memorized typographic rule.

Tutorial 8. Classify a finite relation with repeated vertices

Course-derived: Cambridge, exercise 2. On {a,b,c} let R = {(a,a),(a,b),(b,a),(c,c)}. Determine all seven properties in the definition table.

Solution. Reflexivity fails because (b,b) is missing; irreflexivity fails because (a,a) exists. Symmetry holds because the only off-diagonal pair has its reverse. Antisymmetry and asymmetry both fail on the distinct pair a,b. Transitivity fails because bRaRb would require bRb, which is absent. Seriality holds: a reaches itself or b, b reaches a, and c reaches itself. Inspecting only three distinct vertices would have missed the transitivity failure.

Tutorial 9. A vacuous property is still a property

Original; method: inspect an implication's antecedent. On {a,b,c} classify R = {(a,b)}, and compare it with the empty relation on the same carrier.

Solution. The one-edge relation is irreflexive, antisymmetric, and asymmetric. It is transitive because its only target, b, has no outgoing edge, so no two-edge chain exists. It is not symmetric, reflexive, or serial. The empty relation is additionally symmetric, since no edge can violate the implication. Both remain nonreflexive on this nonempty carrier. If the carrier is empty instead, reflexivity and seriality become vacuously true as well; statements must specify the carrier.

Tutorial 10. A parity relation with a complete proof

Course-derived: Stanford, Binary Relations I. On the integers define aRb when a + b is even. Prove equivalence and determine the classes.

Solution. For any integer a, a + a = 2a, so reflexivity holds. If a + b is even, commutativity makes b + a even, proving symmetry. If a + b = 2r and b + c = 2s, subtract 2b from their sum to obtain a + c = 2(r + s − b), proving transitivity. The integers r + s − b remain integers, which matters to the definition of evenness. Two numbers have an even sum exactly when their parities agree, so the classes are the even integers and the odd integers. Symmetry alone would not have justified the final claim of equivalence.

Tutorial 11. Locate the hidden assumption in a false proof

Course-derived: Stanford, Problem Set 3, Problem Two. A proposed proof chooses arbitrary aRb, reverses it by symmetry, and obtains aRa by transitivity. It concludes that every symmetric transitive relation is reflexive. Explain the defect and repair the statement.

Solution. The argument proves a loop only for elements with an outgoing edge. An isolated element may offer no b to choose. The empty relation on a singleton is a counterexample: symmetry and transitivity hold but its loop is absent. Adding seriality guarantees a witness for every element and makes the argument valid. Alternatively, restrict the carrier to the active domain; the resulting partial equivalence relation becomes an equivalence relation. Choosing arbitrary elements under extra hypotheses cannot establish a claim about all elements without those hypotheses.

Tutorial 12. Cyclicity and right-Euclideanity

Course-derived: Stanford, Binary Relations II and Problem Set 3, Problem Three. Give complete arguments that reflexivity plus either alternative property characterizes equivalence. Give a right-Euclidean relation that is not symmetric.

Solution. For cyclicity, aRa and aRb imply bRa, so symmetry follows. Then aRbRc implies cRa by cyclicity and aRc by symmetry. Conversely, transitivity gives aRc and symmetry reverses it, proving cyclicity of an equivalence relation. For right-Euclideanity, the pair of hypotheses aRb and aRa gives bRa. Given aRbRc, use bRa and bRc with common source b to obtain aRc. Conversely, aRb and aRc give bRaRc by symmetry, hence bRc by transitivity. On {a,b}, R = {(a,b),(b,b)} is right-Euclidean: every source's outgoing set is {b}, and bRb exists. It is not symmetric because (b,a) is missing. Reflexivity was essential to the characterization.

Tutorial 13. Seriality does not create a strict order

Course-derived: Oxford, exercise 4.5; extended distinction. Construct a finite relation that is irreflexive, antisymmetric, and serial. Explain why no finite nonempty strict partial order is serial.

Solution. On {a,b,c} take the directed cycle a → b → c → a. No loops or reverse pairs occur, and every vertex has an outgoing edge, so all requested properties hold. It is not transitive: aRbRc lacks aRc. A finite nonempty strict partial order has a maximal element by applying the minimal-element argument to its dual. That maximal element has no outgoing strict comparison, contradicting seriality. The construction is possible only because transitivity was not one of the requested conditions.

Tutorial 14. A rational equivalence with a nonstandard description

Course-derived: Stanford, Problem Set 3, Problem One. Let H be the rationals having some representation with odd nonzero denominator. On the real numbers define x ∼ y when y − x ∈ H. Prove equivalence and identify [0].

Solution. Zero has denominator 1. If p/q ∈ H, its negative has the same odd denominator. Adding p/q and r/s produces (ps + rq)/(qs), whose denominator is odd, so H is closed under addition and subtraction. These facts prove reflexivity, symmetry, and transitivity of the difference relation. The class of zero is exactly H by substituting zero into the definition, and every class is a translate x + H. The number 3/2 is not in H: if it equalled p/q with odd q, cross multiplication would make the odd integer 3q equal to the even integer 2p. The word “odd” describes the existence of an odd-denominator representation, not the parity of an arbitrary unreduced denominator.

Tutorial 15. Count properties on four labelled elements

Course-derived: Oxford, §4.6. Compute the counts of reflexive, symmetric, antisymmetric, asymmetric, and reflexive symmetric relations on four elements. Count relations that are both symmetric and antisymmetric.

Solution. There are four diagonals and six unordered distinct pairs. Reflexive relations have 12 free off-diagonal entries, giving 212 = 4096. Symmetric relations have ten binary choices, giving 210 = 1024. Antisymmetric relations have four binary diagonal choices and six ternary pair choices, giving 2436 = 11664. Asymmetric relations fix the diagonal and leave the ternary choices, giving 36 = 729. Reflexive symmetric relations give 26 = 64. A symmetric antisymmetric relation can contain only loops, so there are 24 = 16. None of these counts silently includes transitivity.

Tutorial 16. Exact powers of a cycle

Course-derived: Oxford, exercise 4.6; changed instance. On {a,b,c} take R = {(a,b),(b,c),(c,a)}. Compute R2, R3, R ∘ R − 1, R+, and R∗.

Solution. Two steps give (a,c),(b,a),(c,b), while three steps return to the starting vertex, so R3 = IA. The converse moves one step backwards; following it and then R gives exactly the identity. All vertex pairs are reachable in one, two, or three positive steps, so R+ = A × A, and adding zero-length paths changes nothing. The powers are periodic rather than increasing. Truncating the positive closure after R2 would omit every loop.

Tutorial 17. A tight finite closure bound

Course-derived: Cambridge, exercise 6. Why does a directed n-cycle require the Rn term for positive closure, while a directed n-vertex chain does not?

Solution. In the cycle, returning to the starting vertex in positive length first occurs after n edges. Earlier powers therefore miss its diagonal pair. In a chain, every positive path moves strictly forward and uses at most n − 1 edges; no cycle creates a diagonal pair. Both examples obey the general n bound, but the cycle shows it cannot be uniformly reduced for R+. For R∗, identity supplies all diagonal pairs, and the remaining distinct-endpoint paths need at most n − 1 edges.

Tutorial 18. Trace Warshall through a cycle

Original; method: pivot invariant. Start on {a,b,c,d} with R = {(a,b),(b,c),(c,a)}, leaving d isolated. Process pivots in alphabetical order and list the newly added pairs at each stage.

Solution. With internal vertex a allowed, c → a → b adds (c,b). Allowing b uses incoming edges from a,c and the outgoing edge to c, adding (a,c) and (c,c). Allowing c then makes every ordered pair among a,b,c reachable; the new pairs are (a,a),(b,a),(b,b). No edge involving d can be formed, so the final pivot adds nothing. Positive closure is the full square of {a,b,c}, with nine pairs. Reflexive transitive closure additionally has (d,d), giving ten. A zero-length convention should be stated before interpreting a diagonal entry.

Tutorial 19. A single pass with the wrong loop order fails

Original; method: refute an algorithmic shortcut. Consider the loop order i,j,k with all indices increasing and one pass over each entry. Use vertices numbered 0 through 3 and edges 0 → 2, 2 → 3, 3 → 1 to show failure.

Solution. When row 0, column 1 is processed, no middle index yet witnesses reachability: row 0 lacks an edge to 3, and row 2 does not yet contain reachability to 1. Later, processing row 0, column 3 adds 0 → 3 through 2. Later still, processing row 2, column 1 adds 2 → 1 through 3. But the already processed entry (0,1) is not revisited, so the positive path 0 → 2 → 3 → 1 is missed. Warshall's outer-pivot order revisits all endpoint entries whenever a new internal vertex is permitted and avoids this defect.

Tutorial 20. The order of closures matters

Course-derived: Cambridge, exercises 9–10. On {a,b,c} use R = {(a,b),(a,c)} to compare s(t(R)) and t(s(R)). Then determine its equivalence closure.

Solution. No edge starts at b or c, so t(R) = R. Symmetrizing gives four edges, from a to each other vertex and back. It lacks (b,c) and all loops. Symmetrizing first permits paths between every pair and positive closed paths at every vertex, so t(s(R)) = A × A. The equivalence closure is therefore also A × A. For an isolated fourth vertex, positive closure of the symmetrized relation would still omit that vertex's loop; reflexive closure would be required to complete the equivalence relation.

Tutorial 21. When can a partial-order extension exist?

Course-derived: Cambridge, exercise 10; full criterion. Determine exactly when a relation on a finite carrier has a partial-order superset on that same carrier, and describe the least such superset.

Solution. A directed cycle involving at least two distinct vertices is impossible in any partial-order extension: transitivity gives comparisons in both directions between distinct vertices, contradicting antisymmetry. If no such cycle exists, take R∗. It is reflexive and transitive by construction. Two opposite positive paths between distinct vertices would create a prohibited cycle, so it is antisymmetric. Thus R∗ is a partial order. Every partial-order superset contains the identity and every finite input path, so it contains R∗, proving leastness. Original self-loops are allowed. The criterion distinguishes harmless reflexive loops from nontrivial directed cycles.

Tutorial 22. Closure of prime-multiple steps

Course-derived: Cambridge, exercises 8–10. On positive integers let aRb when b = pa for a prime p. Describe the positive and reflexive transitive closures and its equivalence closure.

Solution. A positive path multiplies by one or more primes, so its endpoint ratio is an integer at least 2. Conversely, every such ratio factors into primes, supplying a path. Thus R+ is proper divisibility on positive integers, and R∗ is divisibility including equality. After reversing edges as well, every integer is connected to 1 by successively deleting its prime factors. Hence the equivalence closure has a single class, all positive integers. Positivity excludes complications involving zero and signs; a different carrier would require a fresh argument.

Tutorial 23. Equivalence intersection and union

Course-derived: Cambridge, exercise 7. On {a,b,c} let E have blocks {a,b},{c} and F have blocks {a},{b,c}. Compute their intersection and the equivalence closure of their union.

Solution. Both relations contain every loop. Their only off-diagonal pairs are respectively the two directions between a,b and between b,c, so the intersection is IA. The union has a path a → b → c but omits (a,c), proving it is not itself transitive. Positive closure connects all three vertices in both directions and keeps the existing loops, yielding A × A. Intersection refines the partitions to singleton blocks; closing the union merges them to one block.

Tutorial 24. Classes, quotient objects, and pair counts

Original; method: recover a relation from blocks. A six-element carrier is partitioned into blocks {a,b,c},{d,e},{f}. Write the quotient and count the relation's pairs. Is [a] the same kind of object as a?

Solution. The quotient is the three-element set whose elements are the three displayed blocks. Inside each block every ordered pair is present, including loops, while no cross-block pair exists. The pair count is 32 + 22 + 12 = 14. The class [a] equals {a,b,c} and is also [b] and [c]; it is a set, whereas the original symbol a denotes one carrier element. Counting different representative names would incorrectly produce six quotient elements.

Tutorial 25. Count equivalence relations into exactly two classes

Course-derived: Oxford, partition-counting pattern; extended derivation. On five labelled elements, count equivalence relations with exactly two classes and all equivalence relations.

Solution. Choose a nonempty proper subset as one block. There are 25 − 2 = 30 choices, but each partition is counted twice because either block could be chosen first. Therefore there are 15 two-block partitions. The Stirling recurrence gives the row for five elements as 1,15,25,10,1 for one through five blocks, summing to B5 = 52. The two-block count is not the total count. Labelling the two blocks would restore the factor of two and instead count onto functions to a labelled two-element target.

Tutorial 26. Quotient maps need representative independence

Course-derived: Cornell, Lecture 7. Modulo 6, decide whether the formulas ḡ([a]) =  parity of a, h̄([a]) = a2, and k̄([a]) = [a2] define maps. The middle map targets the integers; the last targets classes modulo 6.

Solution. Equivalent integers differ by a multiple of 6 and hence have equal parity, so the first map is well-defined. The second fails: 1 and 7 represent the same class but their squared integers are 1 and 49. For the third, if a − b = 6t, then a2 − b2 = (a − b)(a + b) is divisible by 6. The squared outputs therefore define the same class, so the last map is well-defined. The target's equality notion determines whether output equality means integer equality or quotient-class equality.

Tutorial 27. Fractions, zero denominators, and a binary operation

Original; method: track cancellation and both representatives. Explain why allowing denominator zero breaks the cross-product equivalence, and prove addition is well-defined for positive-denominator fraction classes.

Solution. With zero denominators allowed, (1,1) relates to (0,0) and (0,0) relates to (2,1) because both cross-products are zero. But (1,1) does not relate to (2,1), so transitivity fails. For valid denominators, let (p,q) ∼ (p′,q′) and (r,s) ∼ (r′,s′). Then pq′ = p′q and rs′ = r′s. Addition produces (ps + rq,qs). Cross multiplication with the primed result gives (ps + rq)q′s′ = psq′s′ + rqq′s′. Substitute the two assumed identities to obtain (p′s′ + r′q′)qs. The outputs are equivalent, and both output denominators are positive. Checking only one representative would leave half of the well-definedness obligation unproved.

Tutorial 28. Collapse a preorder into a partial order

Course-derived: Oxford, preorder example; original quotient extension. On subsets of {1,2,3} let X P Y mean |X| ≤ |Y|. Describe the preorder quotient and its order.

Solution. Cardinality comparison is reflexive and transitive. It is not antisymmetric: {1} and {2} compare both ways but differ. Mutual comparison means equal cardinality, producing four classes, sizes 0, 1, 2, and 3. The quotient order compares these sizes numerically and is the four-element chain. It is well-defined because replacing a subset by another of the same size does not change an inequality. This quotient keeps the information the preorder can distinguish and removes the information it cannot.

Tutorial 29. Strong components and one-way reachability

Original; method: distinguish two closures. With edges a → b, b → a, b → c, and c → d, find mutual-reachability classes and their quotient order. Contrast the equivalence closure of the original edge relation.

Solution. The strongly connected components are {a,b}, {c}, and {d}. Reachability orders them as a three-element chain, with the first preceding both later components. Neither c nor d can reach the first component. Ignoring edge directions instead connects all four vertices, so the equivalence closure has just one class. Directed mutual reachability preserves separate components that undirected connectivity merges. A raw directed edge relation need not be reflexive or transitive, so it is not itself this component order.

Tutorial 30. Strictness from a definition of integer order

Course-derived: Stanford, Problem Set 3, checkpoint and Problem Four. Define a ≺ b when b = a + k for a positive integer k. Prove it is a strict partial order, without assuming the usual order laws as the proof.

Solution. A self-comparison would give a = a + k with positive k, forcing k = 0, a contradiction. For two comparisons, write b = a + k and c = b + l with positive integers k,l. Substitution gives c = a + (k + l), and the sum is positive, proving transitivity. Irreflexivity plus transitivity implies asymmetry by the general theorem, so the relation is a strict order. The proof does not presume transitivity of the symbol it is defining; it derives it from positive-integer addition.

Tutorial 31. Product and lexicographic comparisons

Course-derived: Oxford, §8.2 and exercise 8.2. Compare (1,5) and (2,4) under the two orders on ℕ². Then compare (2,4) and (2,7).

Solution. In the product order, the first pair moves upward in its first coordinate and downward in its second, so neither tuple is below the other. In the lexicographic order, the first coordinate 1 is smaller than 2 and immediately settles the comparison: (1,5) is smaller. For equal first coordinates 2, the second coordinates 4 and 7 decide both product and lexicographic comparison, so (2,4) lies below (2,7) in both. Priority and componentwise dominance are distinct definitions, not two drawings of one order.

Tutorial 32. A Hasse diagram is a cover graph

Course-derived: Stanford, Problem Set 3, Problem Five. Determine the cover relations for natural-number order and power-set inclusion. Explain why the cover relation itself need not be transitive.

Solution. Under the usual natural-number order, b covers a exactly when b = a + 1. A larger gap has an intermediate natural number; a gap of one has none. Under inclusion, Y covers X exactly when X ⊂ Y and |Y ∖ X| = 1. Two or more new elements allow an intermediate set; exactly one allows no intermediate. The cover relation on numbers includes 0 ⋖ 1 and 1 ⋖ 2 but not 0 ⋖ 2, so it is not transitive. Transitivity is recovered by closure, not by the raw cover edges.

Tutorial 33. Recover divisibility order and its extrema

Original; method: inspect covers and upward paths. For divisors of 12, list covers, maximal and minimal elements, height, width, a minimum antichain partition, and a minimum chain partition.

Solution. The carrier is {1,2,3,4,6,12}. Covers are 1 ⋖ 2, 1 ⋖ 3, 2 ⋖ 4, 2 ⋖ 6, 3 ⋖ 6, 4 ⋖ 12, and 6 ⋖ 12. All other strict divisibility pairs are recovered by upward paths. The unique minimal and least element is 1; the unique maximal and greatest is 12. A longest chain is 1,2,4,12, so height is 4. The layers {1},{2,3},{4,6},{12} partition into four antichains, proving the minimum antichain count. The two chains {1,2,4,12} and {3,6} partition the carrier, so width is at most 2; the incomparable pair {2,3} attains 2. Thus this is also a minimum two-chain partition.

Tutorial 34. Unique minimal need not mean least

Original; method: identify the finite hypothesis. Prove the finite implication and give an infinite counterexample.

Solution. In a finite nonempty poset, begin at any element x and move downward while possible. Termination gives a minimal element m ≼ x. If the poset has only one minimal element, every such descent ends there, so that element lies below every x and is least. For the infinite counterexample, take a disjoint union of the integers and a new element p. Retain the usual integer order and compare p only with itself. Every integer has a smaller integer, so none is minimal; p is the unique minimal element. But p is incomparable with every integer and is not least. Finiteness supplied the termination step that fails here.

Tutorial 35. Bounds are ambient objects

Course-derived: Oxford, exercise 8.4; changed instance. In positive integers ordered by divisibility, find the upper-bound set, lower-bound set, supremum, and infimum of {8,12}. Is either bound a maximum or minimum of that subset?

Solution. An upper bound must be divisible by both numbers, so the upper bounds are the positive multiples of 24. The number 24 divides each such bound and itself bounds both inputs, making it their supremum. A lower bound divides both inputs, so the lower bounds are {1,2,4}, with greatest member 4 in divisibility order. Neither 24 nor 4 belongs to {8,12}; neither input divides the other, so the subset has no maximum or minimum. Numerically larger is not the definition of larger in this poset, although lcm and gcd here align with numerical extremality among the relevant bounds.

Tutorial 36. Several minimal upper bounds, no supremum

Course-derived: Oxford, exercise 8.5; fully specified instance. Let the carrier contain all subsets of {1,2,3,4} except the two-element subsets, ordered by inclusion. Find the upper bounds of { {1},{2} } and determine whether a supremum exists.

Solution. Any upper bound must contain both 1 and 2, but {1,2} is missing. The upper bounds in the carrier are {1,2,3}, {1,2,4}, and {1,2,3,4}. The first two are incomparable minimal upper bounds. No upper bound lies below both, so no supremum exists. The carrier has a greatest element, yet it is not a lattice. Having a maximum for the whole carrier does not supply least upper bounds for every pair.

Tutorial 37. A supremum in one carrier and none in another

Course-derived: Oxford, §8.5. For S = {q ∈ ℚ:0<q and q2<2}, explain why the real supremum is √2 and no rational supremum exists.

Solution. Every member is less than √2, making it an upper bound in the reals. For any real a<√2, choose a rational between max(a,0) and √2; it belongs to S and exceeds a, so a is not an upper bound. The needed density fact follows from the Archimedean property: for u<v, choose positive integer n with n(v − u)>1 and integer k = ⌊nu⌋ + 1; then u<k/n<v. Thus √2 is the real supremum. A rational upper bound m cannot equal the irrational √2 and must be larger. Density supplies a rational m′ strictly between them. That smaller rational is still an upper bound, disproving leastness of m. The proof checks membership in the ambient carrier instead of treating a real limit as automatically rational.

Tutorial 38. Supremum without a maximum in lexicographic order

Course-derived: Oxford, exercise 8.6. In lexicographically ordered ℕ², find the supremum of S = {(0,n):n ∈ ℕ} and decide whether it has a maximum.

Solution. Every member has a larger member (0,n + 1), so no maximum exists. An upper bound cannot have first coordinate 0, because any fixed second coordinate is exceeded. Every pair whose first coordinate is at least 1 is an upper bound. The least of those in lexicographic order is (1,0), so it is the supremum. This answer depends on zero belonging to the natural numbers; using positive naturals in the second coordinate would change its least value.

Tutorial 39. Empty sets and lattice completeness

Original; method: apply universal quantification correctly. Determine the supremum and infimum of the empty subset in the power-set lattice of a finite set U. Explain why ordinary real order is not a complete lattice.

Solution. Every subset of U is both an upper and lower bound of the empty family. The least upper bound is therefore the least element, the empty set. The greatest lower bound is the greatest element, U. In ordinary real order the empty set has no supremum because there is no least real number; the whole real carrier also has no real upper bound. Either failure disproves complete-lattice completeness. The theorem that bounded nonempty real subsets have suprema is a different and weaker condition.

Tutorial 40. An order-preserving bijection can fail to be an isomorphism

Course-derived: Oxford, §8.6; original counterexample. Compare the identity map from a two-element antichain to a two-element chain. Then exhibit a genuine divisor/power-set isomorphism.

Solution. The identity map preserves every source comparison because those comparisons are only equalities. It is bijective, but the chain has a strict comparison that the source does not, so it fails order reflection and is not an isomorphism. For divisors of 30, map a divisor to the subset of {2,3,5} consisting of its prime factors. The map is bijective because 30 is squarefree, and one divisor divides another exactly when its factor set is included. Both directions hold, so this map is an order isomorphism. Cardinality and forward monotonicity alone would not prove that.

Tutorial 41. Unit-time scheduling with a sharp lower bound

Course-derived: MIT, §§7.7–7.9; original task graph. Six unit tasks have dependencies A ≺ C, A ≺ D, B ≺ D, C ≺ E, D ≺ E, and D ≺ F. Give a linear extension and an optimal unlimited-processor schedule. Explain the effect of one processor.

Solution. One legal listing is A,B,C,D,E,F; each dependency points forward. Levels are {A,B}, then {C,D}, then {E,F}. Each level consists of mutually independent tasks, and every input of a task finishes in an earlier level. A chain such as A,C,E requires three slots, so the three-level schedule is optimal with unlimited processors. With one processor, six unit tasks require six slots, attained by the linear extension. Height remains a lower bound, but processor capacity prevents attaining it. The graph states precedence, not simultaneous resource availability.

Tutorial 42. Chain–antichain bounds and subsequences

Course-derived: MIT, §7.9. Show that any poset with 25 elements has a chain or an antichain of size at least 5. Apply the reasoning to increasing and decreasing subsequences of a sequence of 25 distinct numbers.

Solution. If both height and width were at most 4, the level partition would have at most four antichains of at most four elements, hence at most 16 elements, a contradiction. More generally 25 ≤ hw makes at least one of h,w at least 5. For the sequence, put an order on positions: i ≼ j when i = j, or when i<j and the value at i is smaller than the value at j. Reflexivity, antisymmetry, and transitivity hold. A chain, read in position order, is an increasing subsequence. An antichain, read in position order, is decreasing because values are distinct and an increasing pair would be comparable. Thus one of the two subsequence types has length at least 5. Distinctness is essential to this strict formulation.

Tutorial 43. Use matching to certify a minimum chain partition

Original; method: construct matching and antichain certificates. For the six-task poset of Problem 41, use comparisons A ≺ C, C ≺ E, and B ≺ D as matching links. Find a chain partition and prove it is minimum.

Solution. On left/right copies, the links are ALCR, CLER, and BLDR. Their left endpoints are distinct and right endpoints are distinct, so they are a matching even though the original vertex C appears on both sides. They produce chains {A,C,E}, {B,D}, and {F}, giving three chains. This is a valid partition but it is not minimum. Add the fourth link DLFR, whose left and right copies are both unused in the matching. The new partition is {A,C,E} and {B,D,F}. The incomparable pair {C,D} forces every chain partition to use at least two chains, so the displayed two-chain partition is minimum and the width is 2. An arbitrary matching establishes a feasible partition; maximum size requires an optimality argument such as this antichain certificate.

Tutorial 44. Well-foundedness and a recursive descent

Course-derived: Cambridge, pp. 40–42; original compact recursion. On ℕ², order argument pairs lexicographically. A recursive procedure on (m,n) may call (m,n − 1) when n>0, or (m − 1,n + 7) when m>0. Prove that recursive descent terminates. Explain why a directed two-cycle invalidates a claim based only on irreflexivity.

Solution. The natural-number order is well-founded, and choosing a minimal first coordinate and then a minimal second coordinate proves well-foundedness of its lexicographic product. The first call decreases the second coordinate while preserving the first; the second decreases the first regardless of its larger second coordinate. Both are strict decreases in that well-founded order, so an infinite call chain is impossible. Nonnegative guards keep the calls inside the carrier, and any branch performing no call terminates its descent. On a two-cycle a → b → a there are no loops, but the nonempty subset {a,b} has no predecessor-free element. Thus irreflexivity alone gives neither well-foundedness nor termination.

Tutorial 45. Lattice identities and a distributivity failure

Original; method: use the order definition of operations. Prove absorption in a lattice and show precisely how distributivity fails in the five-element diamond with bottom 0, top 1, and incomparable middle elements a,b,c.

Solution. The join a ∨ b lies above a. Hence a is a lower bound of the pair a,a ∨ b, and any common lower bound lies below a because a itself is in the pair. Their greatest lower bound is therefore a, proving a ∧ (a ∨ b) = a. In the diamond, the join of any two different middle elements is 1 and their meet is 0. Consequently a ∧ (b ∨ c) = a ∧ 1 = a, but (a ∧ b) ∨ (a ∧ c) = 0 ∨ 0 = 0. The two sides differ because a ≠ 0. A lattice need not inherit the distributive laws of Boolean algebra.

Tutorial 46. Extending a formula to preorders can break it

Original; method: stress-test an omitted hypothesis. On {a,b,c} let the base preorder have equivalence blocks {a,b} and {c}, with no comparisons between the blocks. Define its proposed strict part by comparison plus inequality, and apply the lexicographic formula on pairs. Show that the resulting relation is not transitive.

Solution. The proposed strict part relates a to b and b to a, although these elements are equivalent in the preorder. Consequently (a,a) relates lexicographically to (b,a), and (b,a) relates to (a,c), both through unequal first-coordinate comparisons. But (a,a) does not relate to (a,c): the first coordinates are equal, so the formula requires aPc in the second coordinate, which is false. This is a concrete failure of transitivity. Removing equality from a preorder's relation does not automatically produce an asymmetric strict order. The poset hypothesis, or an appropriately defined asymmetric strict part, prevents the return to an equivalent but unequal first coordinate.

The original four-option numbering is retained for authentic questions. Difficulty labels for original problems are qualitative author judgments, not calibrated response statistics.

Authentic examination questions

Question 1. MSc CS 1405, Q38 — A difference-defined equivalence

Authentic examination · English translation

Original booklet · PDF page 9 · question 38. independently derived; not represented as an official key.

For real x,y, define x∼y exactly when x−y∈A. Which choice of A makes this an equivalence relation?

1.

The integers divisible by 2 or by 3.

2.

{m/n:n∈ℕ,m∈ℤ,m≤n}, with positive denominators.

3.

The integers that are not prime.

4.
{m/2n:n∈ℕ,m∈ℤ}
Read the derivation, conceptual proof and exact option diagnoses

Correct option: 4.

Convert each axiom into a condition on the difference set. The quantifiers range over all real numbers, so every real difference is available. Reflexivity requires 0∈A. If a∈A, the pair (a,0) is related; symmetry makes (0,a) related and requires −a∈A. If a,b∈A, take the triple x=a+b,y=b,z=0. Its first two differences are a,b, so transitivity requires a+b∈A. Necessity is proved using explicit witnesses, rather than assuming a property of a convenient special example.

Conversely, if A contains zero and is closed under negation and addition, equal arguments have difference zero, reversing a related pair negates its difference, and composing related pairs adds their differences. These are exactly reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity. Thus the required condition is that A be an additive subgroup of the reals; it does not require closure under multiplication or division.

For option 4, a negative numerator gives closure under negation and numerator zero gives the identity. Given u=m/2r and v=p/2s, choose k=max(r,s). Then

u+v=m2k−r+p2k−s2k,

whose numerator is an integer. Hence the sum remains dyadic. If natural exponents start at one, the same collection still contains every integer by using an even numerator; the subgroup result is unchanged.

Disprove each other option. Option 1 includes 2 and 3 but excludes their sum 5. Explicitly, 5∼3 and 3∼0, yet ¬(5∼0). Option 2 includes −2 by using a positive denominator one, but all permitted fractions are at most one, so it excludes its negative 2. Thus the related pair (−2,0) has no reverse. Option 3 includes 1, since 1 is not prime, but excludes 1+1=2. The triple 2,1,0 violates transitivity. One counterexample suffices to exclude a universally quantified axiom.

Transfer. With a restricted real carrier, the necessity argument must be rechecked because the witness triple may leave that carrier. Here the original question supplies the entire real line, so the subgroup characterization applies exactly.

This model uses the stated carrier and relation, or the explicitly named countermodel in the proof of a general statement.

Question 2. PhD CS 1405, Q13 — Evaluate a finite relational specification

Authentic examination · English translation

Original booklet · PDF page 7 · question 13. independently derived; not represented as an official key.

The universe is {01,02,03,04,05,06,07,08,09}; girls are {03,06,09}; boys are {02,04,05,08}; the love relation is E={(03,02),(06,08),(04,03),(09,02)}. Evaluate (a) every girl loves exactly one boy; (b) some boy loves some girl.

1.

Only (a).

2.

Only (b).

3.

Both.

4.

Neither.

Read the derivation, conceptual proof and exact option diagnoses

Correct option: 3.

Restrict the relation before checking the quantifiers. The girl-to-boy part has precisely (03,02),(06,08),(09,02). The rows for girls 03, 06 and 09 therefore have boy-target sets {02},{08},{02}. Each is nonempty and has cardinality one. This proves both the existence and uniqueness obligations for statement (a).

In symbols, its condition is

∀g∈G∃b∈B(E(g,b)∧∀b'∈B(E(g,b')⇒b'=b)).

The witnesses may depend on the girl. Girls 03 and 09 sharing boy 02 does not violate this statement: right-uniqueness is not injectivity, and it does not require different rows to select different columns.

For (b), pair (04,03) has a boy in its first position and a girl in its second. It is an explicit witness to ∃b∈B∃g∈GE(b,g). The predicate preserves ordered-pair direction; the girl-to-boy rows alone would not establish this boy-to-girl statement.

Options. Option 3 accepts both true statements. Option 1 incorrectly rejects witness (04,03). Option 2 incorrectly rejects the three singleton girl rows. Option 4 rejects both facts. The domain members 01 and 07 that belong to neither gender group do not create extra obligations in these restricted quantifiers.

Boundary. Replacing “exactly one boy per girl” by “exactly one girl per boy” changes the question and fails on boys with no incoming girl edge. Every translation should name the coordinate being restricted, the witness set and the uniqueness variable.

Question 3. PhD CS 1405, Q23 — A closure operation on equivalences

Authentic examination · English translation

Original booklet · PDF page 8 · question 23. independently derived; not represented as an official key.

If R1 and R2 are equivalence relations on A, which relation below is guaranteed to be an equivalence?

1.
R1−1∩R2−1
2.
R1∪R2
3.
R1−1∪R2−1
4.
R1∪R2−1
Read the derivation, conceptual proof and exact option diagnoses

Correct option: 1.

First eliminate the converse notation. For an equivalence Ri, symmetry gives Ri−1=Ri. All three union options are therefore the same union, while option 1 is the intersection R1∩R2.

For every a∈A, both inputs contain (a,a), so their intersection is reflexive. If (a,b) is in both, its reverse is in both, proving symmetry. If (a,b) and (b,c) are in both, transitivity in each input places (a,c) in both. The intersection is therefore an equivalence. This proof includes the empty carrier by vacuity and does not assume the classes have equal size.

One countermodel excludes the other three options. On {1,2,3}, choose R1 with blocks {1,2},{3} and R2 with blocks {1},{2,3}. Their union has (1,2) and (2,3) but lacks (1,3). It is reflexive and symmetric, yet not transitive. This defeats options 2, 3 and 4 after the converse simplification. A particular pair of equal input relations would have a valid union; the question asks for a guarantee for every pair, which that example cannot establish.

Partition interpretation. The intersection records belonging to the same block under both partitions and thus gives their common refinement. The union links blocks through either partition and can require further merges. Its least equivalence extension is its positive transitive closure, since the input union already contains every loop.
